original_summary: On 8 February 1745, Eugene Aram and Richard Houseman murdered Daniel Clarke in Knaresborough after luring him out to discuss goods he had obtained on credit. Clarke disappeared, and Aram lived openly as a schoolmaster for fourteen years. In 1758, a skeleton was found near Knaresborough, and Houseman’s frightened reaction led to a confession and the discovery of a second skeleton at the exact burial place he identified. Aram was arrested, convicted at York in August 1759, and executed on 16 August after privately confessing his guilt.
seed_elements: On 8 February 1745, Eugene Aram and Richard Houseman take Daniel Clarke out at night and murder him after he has gathered silver and jewels on credit.
Clarke’s disappearance is accepted for fourteen years while Aram continues to work respectably as a teacher in different English towns.
In 1758, a labourer accidentally uncovers a human skeleton at St. Robert’s Cave near Knaresborough, and Aram’s estranged wife says she suspects Aram and Houseman.
When Houseman is asked to handle a bone, he cries, “This is no more Daniel Clarke’s bone than it is mine!” His strange certainty makes people suspect that he has seen the real bones.
Houseman confesses and says the true burial place is slightly farther to the right, with the head lying beyond the first skeleton; people dig there and find a second skeleton exactly in that spot.
Aram is arrested, gives an eloquent written defence, is quickly convicted, privately confesses his guilt, and is executed at York on 16 August 1759.
discarded_elements: The full arguments and historical detail in Aram’s written courtroom defence.
Minor details about Aram’s teaching posts and the towns where he worked.
Excess legal, medical, and period background surrounding the inquest and trial.
Graphic details of Aram’s later actions in his cell; the ending can simply state that he was executed.
Long descriptions of the silver, jewels, cave, and bones beyond what is needed to explain the crime and discovery.
conversion_plan: Write a matter-of-fact third-person retelling in the historical setting, keeping the real names, dates, and sequence of events unchanged. Aim for about 320–380 words at A2 level, using short, clear sentences and retaining the exact Houseman quotation and the precise discovery of the second skeleton. Compress the courtroom defence and other period detail, avoid invented dialogue or motives, and end plainly with Aram’s execution rather than summarizing the whole case again.
